first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Start hands‑only CPR at 100–120 compressions per minute. If an AED is available, attach and follow voice prompts. Continue CPR until emergency services arrive. Do not stop unless the person wakes or you are physically exhausted.
precautions: Do not check for a pulse for more than 10 seconds
If unsure, start CPR – it is better than doing nothing
Use an AED if available – it will only shock if needed
Ensure scene safety before approaching
If the person vomits, roll them to the side, clear the airway, and resume CPR

symptoms: crushing chest pain or pressure, lasting >20 minutes
pain radiating to left arm, jaw, neck, or back
atypical symptoms in women: fatigue, jaw pain, epigastric pain
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Have the person sit down and rest. If not allergic, chew one adult aspirin (325 mg). Loosen tight clothing. Keep them calm. Do not give food or water. If they become unresponsive, begin CPR.
precautions: Do not let the person walk or exert themselves
Do not wait to see if symptoms improve – call 108 immediately
If they have prescribed nitroglycerin, assist with one dose
Note the time of symptom onset – critical for treatment decisions
Know the nearest hospital with a cath lab

symptoms: severe shortness of breath (dyspnoea) at rest or on minimal exertion
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Sit the person upright (high Fowler's position) with legs dangling to reduce venous return. Apply oxygen if available. Do not give fluids. If they have prescribed diuretics, assist with the dose as directed. Monitor breathing and pulse.
precautions: Do not lie the person flat – worsens breathing
Do not give any oral medications without medical advice
If breathing stops, begin CPR
Reassure the person – anxiety worsens the condition
Be prepared for intubation if respiratory failure occurs

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person calm and at rest. Do not give any oral antihypertensives at home (can cause rapid drop). Monitor level of consciousness. If seizures occur, protect from injury. Do not give aspirin (may worsen if stroke).
precautions: Do not lower BP rapidly at home – this can cause stroke
Do not give clonidine or nifedipine without medical supervision
If visual disturbances, protect the person from injury
Monitor for signs of stroke or heart failure
Prepare for IV antihypertensives in hospital

symptoms: sudden, severe, tearing chest or back pain
pulse deficit (difference in BP between arms)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person supine with legs elevated (if not short of breath). Do not give aspirin – it may worsen bleeding. Monitor pulse and blood pressure. Do not give food or drink. Prepare for emergency surgical intervention.
precautions: Do not delay – aortic dissection is rapidly fatal
If chest pain is sudden and severe, do not assume it is a heart attack
Check BP in both arms – a difference >20 mmHg is a warning sign
Do not give thrombolytics
Ensure rapid transport to a centre with cardiac surgery

symptoms: signs of DVT (leg swelling, pain) in some cases
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person sitting upright to ease breathing. Administer oxygen if available. Do not give aspirin – may not help. If they have a known DVT, do not massage the leg. Monitor for cardiac arrest.
precautions: Do not delay – PE can be fatal within minutes
If the person is on anticoagulants, inform the emergency team
Do not give food or water
Keep the person calm to reduce cardiac demand
If they become unresponsive, start CPR

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person lying flat or in a semi‑reclined position. Administer oxygen if available. Do not give any fluid at home. This is a surgical emergency – pericardiocentesis is needed. Rapid transport is critical.
precautions: Do not delay – tamponade can cause sudden cardiac arrest
Do not give diuretics (worsens hypotension)
If the person is on anticoagulants, inform the team
Monitor for loss of consciousness
Prepare for emergency procedure

symptoms: sudden onset of rapid, regular heart rate (150–250 bpm)
first_aid: If the person is unstable (chest pain, hypotension, syncope): call 108 immediately. If stable, try vagal manoeuvres: ask them to bear down (Valsalva) or apply a cold pack to the face. If they become unconscious, start CPR. Do not give adenosine without medical supervision.
precautions: Do not perform vagal manoeuvres in an unstable patient
If the person has a pacemaker or known heart disease, avoid vagal manoeuvres
Do not give any oral medications
Monitor pulse and BP
Prepare for cardioversion if needed

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Start CPR. If an AED is available, apply and shock as advised. Do not stop CPR except for defibrillation. If the person is conscious with VT (rare), do not delay – call 108. This is a shockable rhythm.
precautions: Do not delay defibrillation – every minute decreases survival
Ensure good CPR quality (depth 5–6 cm, rate 100–120/min)
If no AED, continue CPR until ambulance arrives
Do not give food or water
Prepare for advanced cardiac life support

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person lying flat. If they have atropine or a pacemaker, assist as per emergency plan. Do not give beta‑blockers or calcium channel blockers. If they become unconscious, start CPR.
precautions: Do not give any medications that slow the heart further
If they have a pacemaker, check for battery or lead issues
Do not delay – may need emergency pacing
Monitor level of consciousness
Prepare for emergency pacing or atropine

symptoms: seizures occurring without recovery of consciousness
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Place the person on the floor on their side. Protect the head. Do not put anything in the mouth. Time the seizure. If convulsions continue, do not attempt to stop them at home. If the person stops breathing, start CPR. Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam) are given in hospital.
precautions: Do not restrain the person
Do not put fingers or objects in the mouth
If the seizure lasts >5 minutes, this is a medical emergency
If they have a known epilepsy rescue medication (midazolam), administer as directed
Monitor for post‑ictal confusion and injury

symptoms: sudden numbness or weakness of face, arm, or leg (one side)
sudden confusion, trouble speaking or understanding
sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes
sudden severe headache with no known cause
sudden trouble walking, dizziness, loss of balance
first_aid: Call 108 immediately – note the exact time of symptom onset. Keep the person lying flat (or side if vomiting). Do NOT give aspirin, food, or water. If unconscious, place in recovery position. Thrombolysis (tPA) must be given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.
precautions: Do not give aspirin – it may worsen haemorrhagic stroke
Do not let the person 'sleep it off'
Do not give food or drink – risk of aspiration
If the person is on anticoagulants, inform the team
Time is brain – do not delay

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person still and quiet. Do not give aspirin or NSAIDs. Do not give food or water. If vomiting, place on side. This is a neurovascular emergency – CT scan and lumbar puncture are needed. Rapid transport to a centre with neurosurgery.
precautions: Do not delay – re‑bleeding can be fatal
Do not give any painkillers without medical advice
If severe headache, do not assume migraine
Monitor for deterioration in consciousness
Prepare for surgical or endovascular intervention

symptoms: clear fluid from nose or ears (CSF leak)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Stabilise the neck (do not move unless necessary). If unconscious, place in recovery position if breathing. Do not remove a helmet if present. If there is bleeding, apply pressure (avoid if skull fracture is suspected). Monitor breathing and pulse.
precautions: Do not move the person unless absolutely necessary
Do not give any food or water
If CSF leak (clear fluid from nose/ears), do not plug – cover with sterile gauze
Monitor for signs of increased ICP (pupil changes, vomiting)
Do not allow the person to fall asleep without medical evaluation

symptoms: neck or back pain after trauma
numbness, tingling, or weakness in limbs
inability to move arms or legs (paralysis)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do NOT move the person – stabilise the head and neck manually. Do not remove a helmet. If airway is compromised, use jaw thrust (not head tilt). If breathing stops, begin CPR with jaw thrust. Maintain in‑line stabilisation.
precautions: Do not move or twist the neck – can cause permanent paralysis
If the person is lying face down, do not roll over unless airway is compromised
Do not give food or water
If unconscious, open airway with jaw thrust
Transport with spine board

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not delay – bacterial meningitis can be fatal within hours. Keep the person comfortable, reduce light. If vomiting, place on side. Do not give aspirin or NSAIDs – may mask fever. If the rash is non‑blanching, this is a medical emergency. Hospitalisation for IV antibiotics.
precautions: Do not delay – every hour increases risk of death and disability
If neck stiffness with fever, call 108
Do not give food or water if confused
If meningococcal rash, do not wait – go to emergency
Prepare for lumbar puncture and empiric antibiotics

symptoms: severe breathlessness, unable to speak in full sentences
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Sit the person upright. Give 4–8 puffs of salbutamol inhaler through a spacer every 20 minutes. If no inhaler, do not delay. Do not give sedatives. If they stop breathing, begin CPR. Hospitalisation for nebulised bronchodilators, steroids, and oxygen is essential.
precautions: Do not wait – silent chest is an emergency
Do not give sedatives or antihistamines – they depress respiration
Do not use oral steroids at home without medical guidance
If available, give oxygen (if trained)
If they become unconscious, start CPR

symptoms: decreased breath sounds on one side
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is a life‑threatening emergency – needle decompression may be needed (by trained personnel). Do not delay transport. If the person becomes unconscious, begin CPR. Keep them sitting upright if possible. Do not give oxygen if not available.
precautions: Do not delay – tension pneumothorax can cause cardiac arrest
Do not give positive pressure ventilation unless intubated
If a chest drain is not available, transport urgently
Do not give food or water
Prepare for emergency chest drain insertion

symptoms: paradoxical chest wall movement (segment moves inward during inspiration)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Apply a firm pad or large bandage to stabilise the flail segment (or support with a pillow). Do not tape restrictively. Monitor breathing. If respiratory distress worsens, prepare for intubation. Oxygen if available.
precautions: Do not wrap the chest too tightly – can restrict breathing
Do not give food or water
Monitor for signs of pneumothorax or haemothorax
If unconscious, place in recovery position
Rapid transport to a trauma centre

symptoms: coughing up large amounts of bright red blood (>100 ml)
signs of underlying lung disease (TB, bronchiectasis, cancer)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Have the person sit upright and lean forward to cough out blood. Do not lie them flat (risk of aspiration). Do not give anything by mouth. If they become unconscious, place on side. Massive haemoptysis can lead to asphyxiation.
precautions: Do not give cough suppressants – they may cause blood to clot and obstruct airways
Do not give aspirin or anticoagulants
If the person is on anticoagulants, inform the team
Do not delay – urgent bronchoscopy or surgery may be needed
Monitor for airway obstruction

symptoms: often precipitated by sepsis, trauma, or pneumonia
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is a critical condition requiring ICU care. Administer oxygen if available. Keep the person sitting upright. Do not give any fluids at home. If they become unconscious, start CPR. Mechanical ventilation is required.
precautions: Do not delay – ARDS has high mortality
Do not give any medications without medical advice
If the person has a known underlying condition (sepsis), inform the team
Do not give food or water
Prepare for intubation and mechanical ventilation

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person calm – do not lie them flat. Do not try to examine the throat with a spatula – can trigger total airway obstruction. Do not give anything by mouth. If breathing stops, prepare for emergency cricothyroidotomy. This is a paediatric and adult emergency.
precautions: Do not attempt to examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Do not give food or water
If the person is in tripod position, do not force them to lie down
Do not delay – airway can close completely
Prepare for intubation or tracheostomy

first_aid: Call 108 if the child has severe stridor, retractions, or cyanosis. Keep the child calm – do not upset them. Sit them upright. If the child is in distress, do not try to examine the throat. Cool mist from a humidifier or steam may help (but do not delay if severe). Hospitalisation for nebulised adrenaline and steroids.
precautions: Do not give cough syrup – can worsen
Do not give sedatives – depress breathing
Do not force the child to lie down
If stridor is present at rest, it is severe – call 108
Prepare for emergency airway management

symptoms: coughing, wheezing, or inability to speak
the child may have a history of eating small objects or nuts
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the person is conscious but cannot cough effectively, perform back blows and chest thrusts (infants) or Heimlich (adults and children over 1 year). If unconscious, start CPR. Do not try to remove blindly with fingers. Urgent bronchoscopy is needed.
precautions: Do not perform blind finger sweeps – can push object deeper
Do not give food or water
If the object is partially blocking (can speak, cough), encourage coughing
If complete obstruction, act immediately
Transport urgently – bronchoscopy is required

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give insulin at home without medical supervision – this is dangerous. If the person is conscious, give sips of water (not juice). Do not give food. If unconscious, place on side. Hospitalisation for IV fluids, insulin, and electrolyte correction is essential.
precautions: Do not give insulin at home – risk of hypoglycaemia or cerebral oedema
Do not give food or sugary drinks
If you have a glucose meter, check blood sugar
If vomiting, do not give fluids orally – risk of aspiration
Prepare for ICU admission

symptoms: often in Type 2 diabetes with precipitating illness
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is a medical emergency. Do not give insulin at home. Give sips of water if conscious. Do not give food. If unconscious, place on side. Hospitalisation for IV fluids and insulin is needed.
precautions: Do not give insulin at home – risk of hypoglycaemia
Do not give sugary drinks
If the person is on diuretics, inform the team
Monitor for signs of dehydration
Prepare for ICU care

symptoms: known diabetes and on insulin/oral hypoglycaemics
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do NOT give anything by mouth. If you have glucagon injection, administer as directed. If not, apply honey or glucose gel to the gums (not forced). If the person stops breathing, start CPR. Hospitalisation for IV glucose is needed.
precautions: Do not put anything in the mouth of an unconscious person
If the person has a diabetes kit, use the glucagon if available
Do not give insulin – would worsen hypoglycaemia
If they regain consciousness, give fast sugar (juice, glucose) immediately
Monitor blood sugar after recovery

symptoms: precipitated by infection, trauma, or stopping antithyroid drugs
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person calm and cool (reduce fever with cold packs). Do not give any medications without medical supervision. If they have antithyroid drugs, do not stop. Hospitalisation for beta‑blockers, antithyroid drugs, and supportive care is essential.
precautions: Do not give aspirin (may displace thyroid hormones from proteins)
Do not give any herbal supplements
If fever, use paracetamol and cooling
Do not delay – thyroid storm is life‑threatening
Inform the team if the person has Graves' disease

symptoms: precipitated by cold exposure, infection, or stopping thyroxine
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person warm (cover with blankets, but do not use direct heat). Do not give any food or drink. Do not give thyroxine at home. Hospitalisation for IV thyroid hormone and supportive care is essential.
precautions: Do not use heating pads directly – can cause burns
Do not give sedatives – can worsen respiratory depression
If the person is on thyroxine, inform the team
Monitor for respiratory failure
Prepare for ICU admission

symptoms: precipitated by infection, surgery, or stress in those on steroids
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the person has a known adrenal insufficiency and a steroid emergency kit, administer hydrocortisone IM/IV as directed. If not, do not delay. Do not give food or water if vomiting. Hospitalisation for IV steroids, fluids, and glucose is essential.
precautions: Do not stop steroids suddenly – can precipitate crisis
If the person is on steroids, they may need stress doses
Do not give fluids if vomiting – risk of aspiration
If they have a MedicAlert bracelet, check it
Prepare for ICU care

symptoms: history of malignancy, hyperparathyroidism, or excessive Vitamin D
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person well‑hydrated (give oral fluids if conscious and not vomiting). Do not give calcium supplements. If they are on diuretics, stop thiazides. Hospitalisation for IV fluids, bisphosphonates, and calcitonin is needed.
precautions: Do not give calcium or Vitamin D supplements
If vomiting, do not give oral fluids
Monitor for cardiac arrhythmias
If on lithium or thiazides, inform the team
Prepare for emergency treatment

symptoms: increased risk in marathon runners, psychogenic polydipsia, or SIADH
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give large amounts of plain water. If conscious and not vomiting, give salty snacks or ORS. If the person has seizures, protect from injury. Hospitalisation for controlled correction of sodium with hypertonic saline is essential.
precautions: Do not give large volumes of plain water
Do not correct sodium too rapidly (risk of central pontine myelinolysis)
If the person is on diuretics, inform the team
Monitor for signs of cerebral oedema
If coma, prepare for ICU

symptoms: ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS)
risk factors: renal failure, ACE inhibitors, potassium supplements
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the person is on potassium supplements, stop them. Do not give any oral medications at home. If the person has cardiac arrest, start CPR. Hospitalisation for emergency treatment: calcium gluconate (cardioprotection), insulin+glucose, sodium bicarbonate, and dialysis.
precautions: Do not give potassium supplements
Do not use salt substitutes (KCl)
If ECG changes or weakness, this is life‑threatening
If on ACE inhibitors or ARBs, inform the team
Prepare for emergency dialysis

symptoms: ECG: flattened T waves, U waves
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the person is conscious and not vomiting, give potassium‑rich foods (banana, coconut water) – but this will not correct severe hypokalaemia. Do not give potassium supplements without medical supervision. Hospitalisation for IV or oral potassium is needed.
precautions: Do not give potassium supplements without ECG monitoring
If the person is on diuretics, stop them temporarily
Monitor for arrhythmias
If respiratory weakness, prepare for ventilation
Do not delay – cardiac arrest risk

symptoms: sudden severe epigastric pain (radiating to back)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give food or water. Do not give any painkillers without medical advice (may mask symptoms). If vomiting, place on side. Hospitalisation for IV fluids, pain management, and fasting is essential. Monitor for complications.
precautions: Do not give food or water – may worsen
If the person is on alcohol, inform the team
Do not give aspirin or NSAIDs without medical advice
If severe pain, do not delay
Prepare for ICU if organ failure

symptoms: severe right upper quadrant pain (biliary colic) lasting >6 hours
positive Murphy's sign (pain on deep inspiration)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give food or water. Do not give painkillers before medical evaluation. If vomiting, place on side. Hospitalisation for IV antibiotics and possible emergency cholecystectomy.
precautions: Do not give food or water – may need surgery
If pain is severe, do not delay
Do not give aspirin or NSAIDs without medical advice
If jaundice, inform the team
Prepare for surgery

symptoms: pain starting in the periumbilical area, migrating to the right lower quadrant (McBurney's point)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give food or water. Do not give painkillers – may mask symptoms. If vomiting, place on side. Hospitalisation for surgical evaluation. Do not delay – perforation leads to peritonitis.
precautions: Do not give food or water – may need surgery
Do not give painkillers before surgical evaluation
If pain is severe, do not delay
Do not apply heat to the abdomen – can cause perforation
Prepare for appendectomy

symptoms: constipation and obstipation (no flatus or stool)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give food or water. Do not give laxatives – can cause perforation. If vomiting, place on side. Hospitalisation for NG tube decompression, IV fluids, and possible surgery. Do not delay.
precautions: Do not give food or water
Do not give laxatives or enemas
If vomiting, place on side
Do not use heat on abdomen
Monitor for signs of peritonitis (rigid abdomen)

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person lying flat with legs elevated. Do not give food or water. Do not give aspirin – may worsen bleeding. If vomiting, turn head to side. Hospitalisation for urgent endoscopy, blood transfusion, and IV fluids is essential.
precautions: Do not give food or water
Do not give any antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs
If the person is on warfarin, inform the team
Monitor for loss of consciousness
Prepare for blood transfusion

symptoms: sudden massive haematemesis (vomiting large amounts of blood)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Lay the person flat. Do not give food or water. If vomiting, side position. Do not give aspirin. Hospitalisation for urgent endoscopy with band ligation, IV fluids, and blood transfusion is essential.
precautions: Do not give food or water
If the person has cirrhosis, this is a known risk
Do not give any medications without medical advice
Monitor for airway protection – risk of aspiration
Prepare for emergency endoscopy

symptoms: sudden decrease in urine output (<400 ml/day or <0.5 ml/kg/hr)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Restrict fluid intake. Do not give any over‑the‑counter medications (especially NSAIDs). If the person has a known cause (sepsis, dehydration, nephrotoxins), inform the team. Hospitalisation for dialysis and supportive care.
precautions: Do not give NSAIDs – worsen renal function
Do not give potassium‑rich foods or supplements
If the person is on diuretics, stop (unless prescribed for AKI)
Monitor for fluid overload (breathlessness)
Prepare for dialysis

symptoms: severe muscle pain (especially calves, thighs, lower back)
caused by crush injury, prolonged immobilisation, statin use, or drugs
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give any food or water (may need IV fluids). If the person has a crush injury, do not remove the crushed object without medical supervision. Hospitalisation for aggressive IV hydration, urine alkalinisation, and monitoring of renal function is needed.
precautions: Do not give NSAIDs – worsen kidney injury
If on statins, stop them
Do not give potassium supplements (may cause hyperkalaemia)
If the urine is dark, this is an emergency
Prepare for dialysis if severe

symptoms: generalised tonic‑clonic seizures in a pregnant or postpartum woman
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Protect from injury, place on side. Do not put anything in the mouth. Do not give any oral medications. Hospitalisation for IV magnesium sulfate, antihypertensives, and immediate delivery if indicated. Do not delay.
precautions: Do not give oral medications – may aspirate
Do not restrain – can cause injury
If seizures do not stop, this is a medical emergency
Prepare for immediate delivery
Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice – available in all government hospitals

symptoms: heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery (soaking 1 pad per hour or more)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the woman is still in the delivery room, the medical team will manage. If at home, lie her flat, elevate legs, and apply fundal massage (to contract the uterus). Do not give anything by mouth. Hospitalisation for IV fluids, oxytocin, and blood transfusion is essential.
precautions: Do not delay – PPH is a leading cause of maternal death
If the woman is at home, call 108
Do not give food or water
If you are trained, do uterine massage
Prepare for blood transfusion and possible surgery

symptoms: sudden severe lower abdominal pain (one‑sided, sharp, stabbing)
vaginal bleeding (may be light or heavy)
shoulder tip pain (referred pain from blood tracking to the diaphragm)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Lay the woman flat and keep her still. Do not give food or water. Do not give painkillers. If she becomes unconscious, place on side. Hospitalisation for emergency surgery. This is life‑threatening.
precautions: Do not delay – ruptured ectopic is fatal if untreated
Do not give food or water – may need surgery
If the woman is pregnant and has sudden pain, call 108
Do not try to treat at home
Prepare for emergency laparotomy

symptoms: sudden severe one‑sided lower abdominal pain
usually in women with ovarian cysts or PCOS
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give food or water (may need surgery). Do not give painkillers – may mask symptoms. If vomiting, side position. Hospitalisation for emergency laparoscopic detorsion.
precautions: Do not delay – ovary can die within 4‑6 hours
Do not give painkillers before surgical evaluation
If the woman has a known cyst, be alert
Do not apply heat
Prepare for surgery

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is a life‑threatening obstetric emergency. Lay the woman flat. Do not give food or water. Prepare for emergency C‑section and possible hysterectomy. Do not delay.
precautions: Do not delay – uterine rupture is fatal for mother and baby
If the woman has a previous C‑section scar, be alert
Do not give food or water
Prepare for blood transfusion
Emergency surgical team needed

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Lay the woman on her side. Do not give food or water. Do not give painkillers. Hospitalisation for immediate delivery. This is an obstetric emergency.
precautions: Do not delay – abruption can cause fetal death and maternal shock
If bleeding is concealed, it is even more dangerous
Do not give food or water
Prepare for emergency C‑section
Blood transfusion readiness

symptoms: umbilical cord visible in the vagina or perineum after membrane rupture
fetal heart rate decelerations (variable or prolonged)
the cord may be pulsating or not
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not push the cord back. If possible, use a sterile gloved hand to lift the presenting part off the cord (relieve pressure). Place the mother in knee‑chest or Trendelenburg position. Do not give anything by mouth. Emergency C‑section is needed.
precautions: Do not push the cord back – worsens compression
Do not give food or water
Do not delay – time is critical
If the cord is not pulsating, this is a neonatal emergency
Prepare for emergency delivery

symptoms: occurs during labour, delivery, or immediately postpartum
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is a catastrophic obstetric emergency. If cardiac arrest occurs, start CPR. Do not give any oral medications. Hospitalisation for ICU care, mechanical ventilation, blood products, and management of DIC is needed. Survival is low.
precautions: Do not delay – AFE is often fatal
If the woman is in labour and has sudden collapse, call 108
Do not give food or water
Prepare for massive blood transfusion
This is a medical emergency requiring multidisciplinary care

symptoms: large areas of skin with deep burns (white, charred, or blistered)
severe pain (or no pain in 3rd degree)
inhalation injury (singed nasal hairs, hoarse voice, sooty sputum)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Cool the burn with running water for 20 minutes. Do NOT use ice. Remove jewellery. Cover with a clean, moist cloth. Do not apply any ointments. Keep the person warm (to prevent hypothermia). If inhalation injury, sit upright. Hospitalisation for fluid resuscitation, wound care, and possible intubation.
precautions: Do not apply ice – worsens damage
Do not use butter, toothpaste, or oil
Do not remove clothing stuck to the burn
If the person has inhalation injury, do not lie flat
Prepare for ICU care

symptoms: severe pain, swelling, deformity in the crushed area
pale or blue skin distal to the injury
absent pulse distal to the injury (vascular compromise)
signs of compartment syndrome (tense, shiny skin, severe pain on passive stretch)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not remove the crushing object unless trained – may cause reperfusion injury and cardiac arrest. If you must remove, be prepared for crush syndrome. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for IV fluids, fasciotomy, and dialysis may be needed.
precautions: Do not remove heavy crushing objects without medical support
Do not give food or water
If the limb is pale, do not elevate
Monitor for signs of rhabdomyolysis
Prepare for emergency surgery

symptoms: complete severance of a limb or digit
the amputated part may be recovered or not
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Control bleeding with a tourniquet (if life‑threatening) or direct pressure. Do not put the amputated part directly on ice – wrap it in a clean moist cloth, place in a sealed bag, then in another container with ice. Bring it to the hospital. Do not give food or water.
precautions: Do not place the amputated part directly on ice
Do not wash the amputated part
Do not give food or water
If you use a tourniquet, note the time of application
Time is critical for reattachment

symptoms: sucking chest wound (air entering through the wound)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not remove the object. Cover an open wound with a non‑porous dressing (plastic) taped on three sides to allow air to escape but not enter. Keep the person sitting upright. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for surgery is essential.
precautions: Do not remove the impaled object
Do not apply pressure that occludes the wound completely – risk of tension pneumothorax
Do not give food or water
Monitor for tension pneumothorax
Prepare for emergency surgery

symptoms: signs of internal bleeding (hypotension, tachycardia, pallor)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not remove the object. If organs are protruding, do not push them back – cover with a moist sterile dressing. Do not give food or water. Place the person in a supine position with knees bent. Hospitalisation for emergency surgery.
precautions: Do not remove the impaled object
Do not push protruding organs back
Do not give food or water
If vomiting, place on side
Prepare for emergency laparotomy

symptoms: shortening or rotation of a leg
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Stabilise the pelvis with a pelvic binder or sheet wrapped snugly around the hips. Do not log roll unless necessary. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for trauma team and possible surgery.
precautions: Do not move the person unnecessarily
Do not give food or water
If the person is unstable, treat for shock
Do not apply pressure to the pelvis without stabilisation
Prepare for pelvic angiography or surgery

symptoms: severe thigh pain, deformity (shortened, rotated leg)
signs of shock (if open or large blood loss)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Immobilise the leg with a splint (traction splint if available). Do not try to straighten the bone. If open, cover the wound. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for traction or surgery.
precautions: Do not try to straighten or align the bone
Do not give food or water
If you have a traction splint, use it
Monitor for signs of fat embolism (confusion, petechiae, respiratory distress)
Prepare for surgery

symptoms: petechial rash (especially on chest, axillae, conjunctiva)
occurs 24–72 hours after long bone or pelvic fractures
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is a complication of trauma. Do not give any oral medications. Keep the person in a semi‑upright position. Hospitalisation for ICU care, supportive ventilation, and management of the underlying fracture is essential.
precautions: Do not delay – fat embolism can be fatal
If the person has a fracture and develops confusion, call 108
Do not give food or water
Monitor oxygen saturation
Prepare for ICU admission

symptoms: severe pain out of proportion to the injury
pain on passive stretch of the muscles
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Remove any constricting bandages or casts. Keep the limb at heart level (do not elevate, as this reduces perfusion). Do not apply ice. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for emergency fasciotomy.
precautions: Do not elevate the limb – worsens ischaemia
Do not apply heat or ice
Do not give food or water
Time is muscle – fasciotomy within 6 hours is ideal
Prepare for emergency surgery

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the person is conscious, keep them sitting upright. Do not blow the nose (risk of pneumocephalus). Do not give food or water – may need surgery. If there is bleeding, apply pressure (avoid if fracture is suspected). Hospitalisation for facial reconstruction.
precautions: Do not blow the nose
Do not give food or water
Do not apply pressure to the nose if CSF leak is suspected
Monitor for airway obstruction
Prepare for facial surgery

symptoms: visible laceration or foreign body in the eye
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do NOT apply pressure to the eye. Protect the eye with a rigid shield (e.g., paper cup taped over the eye). Do not irrigate. Do not give aspirin. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for emergency ophthalmology surgery.
precautions: Do not press on the eye
Do not remove any foreign body
Do not apply eye drops
Do not give food or water
Prepare for emergency surgery

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is an ophthalmic emergency. Do not give any eye drops without medical advice. Keep the person calm and in a darkened room. Do not give food or water if vomiting. Hospitalisation for urgent pressure‑lowering therapy and possible laser iridotomy.
precautions: Do not use mydriatic eye drops (dilating drops) – worsens
Do not delay – vision can be lost in hours
Do not give aspirin
If nausea, place on side
Prepare for emergency ophthalmology care

symptoms: shadow or curtain in the peripheral or central visual field
first_aid: Call an ophthalmologist immediately or go to the nearest eye hospital. This is a medical emergency. Avoid head movements that may worsen the detachment. Do not give any medications. Do not rub the eye. Surgical repair is needed.
precautions: Do not delay – retinal detachment can lead to permanent blindness
Do not rub the eye
Do not give aspirin
Do not do heavy lifting
Prepare for emergency surgery (scleral buckle or vitrectomy)

symptoms: chemical splatter or powder in the eye
alkali burns are more severe than acid burns
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Immediately rinse the eye with copious amounts of water or saline for at least 20 minutes. Hold the eyelid open. Do not stop to neutralise. Continue rinsing while transporting to hospital. Do not apply any ointment. Hospitalisation for further irrigation and specialist care.
precautions: Do not delay – alkali burns can penetrate the eye quickly
Do not try to neutralise with acid/alkali – use water only
Do not apply any ointment before irrigation
Do not rub the eye
If dry powder, brush it off before irrigating

symptoms: hot, dry skin (may be sweaty in exertional type)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Move to a cool place. Remove clothing. Cool rapidly using any method: immerse in cold water, apply ice packs to neck, armpits, groin, and fan vigorously. Do not give anything by mouth if unconscious. Do not give aspirin or paracetamol. Hospitalisation for IV fluids and cooling.
precautions: Do not use ice directly on skin without a cloth – can cause frostbite
Do not give oral medications
Do not delay – heat stroke has high mortality
If conscious, give cool water (not iced)
Monitor for seizures

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Move to a warm, dry place. Remove wet clothing. Use passive warming (blankets) and active warming (warm compresses on chest, neck, groin – avoid extremities). Do not give alcohol. Do not give hot drinks or food if unconscious. If not breathing, start CPR. Hospitalisation for active rewarming.
precautions: Do not use direct heat (heating pads) on arms and legs – can cause afterdrop
Do not give alcohol
Do not rub or massage the person – can cause cardiac arrhythmias
Do not give food or water if unconscious
Handle gently – risk of ventricular fibrillation

symptoms: white, waxy, numb, or hard skin
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Immerse the affected part in warm water (37–40°C, not hot) for 15–30 minutes. Do not rub or massage. Do not use dry heat. Do not walk on affected feet. Elevate the limb and cover with dry, sterile gauze. Hospitalisation for wound care and possible amputation.
precautions: Do not rub or massage – damages tissue
Do not use direct heat (fire, heating pad) – burns
Do not thaw if there is a risk of refreezing
Do not walk on frostbitten feet
Prepare for surgical debridement or amputation

symptoms: dry cough progressing to frothy sputum
occurs at altitudes >2,500 m, often within 2–4 days of ascent
first_aid: Descend immediately to a lower altitude (this is the most important treatment). Administer oxygen if available. If no descent possible, use a portable hyperbaric bag. Do not give sleeping pills. Hospitalisation for oxygen, diuretics, and possibly nifedipine. Do not delay.
precautions: Do not stay at altitude – descent is the priority
Do not give sedatives
Do not give alcohol
Do not smoke
If symptoms, do not ascend further

first_aid: Descend immediately – this is a medical emergency. Administer oxygen. Give dexamethasone (if available and trained). Do not give sedatives. Hospitalisation for further management. Do not leave the person alone.
precautions: Do not stay at altitude – descend
Do not give sedatives
Do not give alcohol
If the person is confused, do not leave them
Prepare for helicopter evacuation if possible

symptoms: occurs after scuba diving or rapid ascent from depth
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Administer 100% oxygen if available. Do not give any oral fluids. Do not give painkillers without medical advice. Recompress in a hyperbaric chamber as soon as possible. Keep the person supine. Do not fly.
precautions: Do not delay – recompression is time‑critical
Do not give alcohol or sedatives
Do not fly (makes it worse)
If the person is unconscious, place on side
Prepare for emergency hyperbaric treatment

symptoms: symptoms may appear hours after the event
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. All near‑drowning victims must be evaluated, even if they seemed fine initially. If the person has respiratory distress, sit them upright. Administer oxygen if available. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for observation and possible oxygen therapy.
precautions: Do not assume the person is fine because they coughed up water
Do not give food or water
Monitor for respiratory distress
If symptoms worsen, call 108
Prepare for hospital admission

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Check for breathing and pulse – if absent, start CPR. Treat burns. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for cardiac monitoring, neurological evaluation, and treatment of burns. Lightning survivors need thorough assessment.
precautions: Do not delay – cardiac arrest is common
Do not assume the person is dead – start CPR
Do not give food or water if unconscious
Monitor for arrhythmias
Prepare for ICU care

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Ensure the power source is turned off. Do not touch the person if they are still connected. If not breathing, start CPR. Treat burns. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for cardiac monitoring, rhabdomyolysis monitoring, and burn care.
precautions: Do not touch the person until the power is off
Do not give food or water if unconscious
Monitor for cardiac arrhythmias
If the person is on a ladder, do not move them until spinal injury is ruled out
Prepare for ICU care

symptoms: cherry‑red skin (classic but not always present)
history of being in an enclosed space with a fuel‑burning appliance
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Move the person to fresh air immediately. If not breathing, start CPR. Administer 100% oxygen if available. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy if available. Do not re‑enter the area.
precautions: Do not stay in the contaminated area – risk to rescuer
Do not give food or water if unconscious
Do not use smoke alarms as a replacement for CO detectors
If the person is confused, do not leave them
Prepare for hyperbaric oxygen if indicated

symptoms: respiratory depression (slow, shallow breathing, or apnea)
history of opioid use (heroin, morphine, methadone)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If you have naloxone (Narcan) and are trained, administer intranasal or IM. Start CPR if no breathing. Place on side. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for observation and supportive care.
precautions: Do not give food or water – risk of aspiration
Do not use opioids to 'reverse' – only naloxone works
If you give naloxone, stay with the person until help arrives (may wear off)
Do not delay calling 108
Prepare for ventilatory support

symptoms: respiratory depression (mild to severe, if combined with alcohol)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Maintain airway – place on side. If not breathing, start CPR. Do not give food or water. Flumazenil can reverse but is not given at home – carries seizure risk. Hospitalisation for supportive care and possible flumazenil.
precautions: Do not give any sedatives
Do not give food or water
Monitor for respiratory depression
If the person is on other CNS depressants (alcohol), inform the team
Prepare for ICU care

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not induce vomiting. If unconscious, place on side. If not breathing, start CPR. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for cardiac monitoring, sodium bicarbonate (for arrhythmias), and supportive care. TCA overdose is life‑threatening.
precautions: Do not induce vomiting – risk of aspiration
Do not give any medications at home
Monitor for seizures
If the person has cardiac symptoms, this is critical
Prepare for ICU and possible intubation

symptoms: then right upper quadrant pain (liver damage)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately or go to hospital. If within 1 hour of ingestion, you may be given activated charcoal. Do not induce vomiting. Hospitalisation for N‑acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment – this is time‑critical (best within 8 hours). Do not delay.
precautions: Do not induce vomiting at home
Do not give any other medications
Do not assume it's mild – paracetamol toxicity is delayed
If the person is chronic alcohol user, the toxic dose is lower
Prepare for IV NAC

symptoms: DUMBELLS: Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis (pinpoint pupils), Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation, Sweating
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Move the person to fresh air. If on skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash with soap and water. Do not induce vomiting. If not breathing, start CPR. Hospitalisation for atropine and pralidoxime. This is a life‑threatening emergency.
precautions: Do not induce vomiting (risk of aspiration)
Do not give food or water if unconscious
Wear gloves if washing the person – secondary exposure risk
If the person has a chemical smell, inform the team
Prepare for atropine therapy

symptoms: severe burning pain in the mouth, throat, and chest
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do NOT induce vomiting – can cause further burns. Do not attempt to neutralise (produces heat). If the person is conscious, give small sips of water or milk to dilute. Do not give charcoal. Hospitalisation for endoscopy and supportive care.
precautions: Do not induce vomiting – can cause perforation
Do not give acid/alkali neutralisers
Do not give charcoal
If the person has stridor, airway obstruction is imminent
Prepare for emergency endoscopy

symptoms: history of snake bite (especially krait, cobra)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Keep the person calm and immobilise the bitten limb. Do NOT cut or suck the wound. Do NOT apply a tourniquet. Rush to a government hospital – anti‑snake venom (ASV) is available free. Do not give food or water if swallowing is difficult.
precautions: Do not delay – neurotoxic paralysis can involve respiratory muscles
Do not give herbal remedies
Do not apply ice
Do not give food or water if dysphagia
Prepare for mechanical ventilation

symptoms: bleeding from gums, puncture sites, or wounds
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Immobilise the limb. Do not cut or suck. Do not apply a tourniquet. Rush to a government hospital for ASV. Do not give aspirin or NSAIDs (increase bleeding). Prepare for blood transfusion if needed.
precautions: Do not give aspirin or NSAIDs
Do not delay – haemotoxic envenoming can cause DIC
Do not give any herbal remedies
If the person has bleeding, apply pressure
Prepare for ASV and blood products

symptoms: severe pain at the sting site
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Apply a cold pack to the sting site. Do not cut or suck. Do not apply tourniquet. Hospitalisation for antivenom and supportive care (prazosin for sympathetic overactivity). Children need urgent care.
precautions: Do not delay – scorpion stings can be fatal in children
Do not give aspirin
Do not apply ice directly – wrap in cloth
If the person has breathing difficulty, sit upright
Prepare for ICU care

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the person has an EpiPen, administer it IM in the lateral thigh (hold for 3 seconds). Lay flat with legs elevated (if breathing is not compromised). If breathing is difficult, sit them upright. Give a second dose after 5–15 minutes if no improvement. If not breathing, start CPR.
precautions: Do not give oral medications – may aspirate
Do not delay using the EpiPen
Do not give antihistamines as the primary treatment – they are too slow
If symptoms worsen, call 108
Prepare for ICU care

symptoms: cold, clammy skin or warm, flushed skin
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. If the person is not breathing, start CPR. Do not give food or water. Keep them warm. Hospitalisation for IV antibiotics, IV fluids, and vasopressors. Septic shock has high mortality – do not delay.
precautions: Do not give oral antibiotics at home
Do not give food or water
If the person has a source of infection, inform the team
Monitor for signs of organ failure
Prepare for ICU care

symptoms: often associated with tampon use, wounds, or surgery
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Remove any tampon or foreign body if present. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for IV fluids, antibiotics, and vasopressors. This is a life‑threatening emergency.
precautions: Do not delay – TSS can be fatal
If the person has a tampon, remove it
Do not give aspirin or NSAIDs
Do not give food or water
Prepare for ICU care

symptoms: high fever, severe headache, retro‑orbital pain
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do NOT give aspirin or ibuprofen – use only paracetamol. Give oral fluids if conscious. If there is bleeding, apply pressure. Hospitalisation for IV fluids and monitoring is essential. Dengue shock syndrome is life‑threatening.
precautions: Do not give aspirin or ibuprofen (increases bleeding)
Do not give food or water if vomiting
If the person is lethargic, do not delay
Monitor urine output
Prepare for ICU care

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give any antimalarials at home without diagnosis. If the person is unconscious, place on side. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for IV artesunate, supportive care, and monitoring. Falciparum malaria is a medical emergency.
precautions: Do not give oral antimalarials at home – may cause vomiting
Do not delay – cerebral malaria can be fatal
If the person has seizures, protect from injury
Do not give aspirin
Prepare for ICU care

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not delay – this is a medical emergency. If the rash does not fade with a glass, immediate antibiotics are needed. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for IV antibiotics (penicillin) and ICU care.
precautions: Do not delay – meningococcaemia can be fatal within hours
If the rash is non‑blanching, call 108 immediately
Do not give aspirin
Do not give food or water if unconscious
Prepare for ICU care and antibiotics

symptoms: severe pain at the wound site (out of proportion)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. This is a surgical emergency. Do not apply any ointment. Do not give food or water. Hospitalisation for surgical debridement, antibiotics (penicillin, clindamycin), and hyperbaric oxygen. Do not delay.
precautions: Do not delay – gas gangrene can be fatal in 24–48 hours
Do not apply heat
Do not give food or water
Do not give painkillers without medical advice – may mask symptoms
Prepare for emergency surgery

symptoms: occurs in adolescents and young adults
first_aid: Call 108 immediately – this is a surgical emergency. Do not give painkillers – may mask the need for surgery. Do not apply heat. If possible, gently elevate the scrotum. Hospitalisation for emergency surgery (detorsion and orchidopexy). Time is testicle – necrosis occurs within 4–6 hours.
precautions: Do not delay – testicle can die within 4–6 hours
Do not give painkillers before surgical evaluation
Do not apply heat
If the person has a history of intermittent pain, still go to emergency
Prepare for surgery

symptoms: distal glans is firm, corpora cavernosa rigid
can cause ischaemic injury and fibrosis
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not attempt to treat with ice or exercise at home. Do not wait – this is a urological emergency. Hospitalisation for aspiration and injection of phenylephrine. Do not give food or water.
precautions: Do not delay – ischaemic priapism can cause permanent erectile dysfunction
Do not apply ice without medical advice
Do not give painkillers – may mask
If the person has sickle cell disease, inform the team
Prepare for urological intervention

symptoms: inability to urinate despite full bladder
first_aid: Call 108 immediately or go to the emergency department. Do not give any medications. Do not try to force urination – can cause rupture. Hospitalisation for Foley catheterisation. This is a urological emergency.
precautions: Do not force urination – risk of bladder rupture
Do not give diuretics – worsens
Do not give food or water
Do not apply heat to the abdomen
Prepare for catheterisation

first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not leave the person alone if they are a danger to themselves or others. Speak calmly and avoid confrontation. Do not restrain unless necessary for safety – can cause injury. Do not give any oral medications. Hospitalisation for psychiatric assessment and sedation.
precautions: Do not argue with delusions – validate feelings
Do not leave the person alone if suicidal or violent
Do not give any medications without medical advice
If the person has a weapon, call police
Prepare for psychiatric evaluation and sedation

symptoms: talking about wanting to die or kill oneself
sudden calmness after severe depression (may have decided)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not leave the person alone. Remove access to means (medications, sharp objects, weapons). Listen without judgment – do not dismiss their feelings. Stay with them until professional help arrives. If they have a plan, this is a medical emergency.
precautions: Do not leave the person alone
Do not argue or lecture
Do not promise to keep it a secret
If they have a weapon, call police
Take them to the nearest hospital emergency or call 108

first_aid: Ensure your own safety. Do not approach if they have a weapon. Call 108 and police if needed. Speak calmly and clearly. Give space. Do not argue. If necessary, seclusion or restraint by trained personnel is used in hospital. Do not attempt to restrain alone.
precautions: Do not confront the person alone
Do not argue
Remove bystanders from the area
Do not use physical restraint unless trained
If the person is a danger to others, call authorities

symptoms: often due to infection, metabolic disturbance, medication, or hypoxia
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not leave the person alone. Remove any hazards. Do not give any medications. If the person is agitated, speak calmly and reduce stimulation. Hospitalisation to identify and treat the underlying cause.
precautions: Do not assume dementia – delirium is reversible
Do not give sedatives without medical advice
Do not leave the person unattended
If the person is on new medications, inform the team
Prepare for diagnostic workup

symptoms: sudden, severe abdominal or back pain (tearing)
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give food or water. Lay the person flat. Do not give aspirin. Hospitalisation for emergency surgery. This is a surgical emergency with very high mortality.
precautions: Do not delay – ruptured AAA is fatal without surgery
Do not give food or water
Do not give painkillers – may mask
If the person has a known AAA, inform the team
Prepare for emergency surgery

symptoms: sudden severe abdominal pain (out of proportion to physical findings)
often in elderly with cardiovascular disease
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Do not give food or water. Do not give painkillers – may mask. Hospitalisation for CT angiography and emergency surgery. This is a surgical emergency.
precautions: Do not delay – mesenteric ischaemia is often fatal
Do not give food or water
Do not give painkillers before surgical evaluation
If the person has atrial fibrillation, inform the team
Prepare for emergency laparotomy

symptoms: swelling of face, lips, tongue, throat
occurring within minutes to hours after taking a medication
first_aid: Call 108 immediately. Stop the medication. If the person has an EpiPen, administer it. If not, keep them comfortable. If breathing difficulty, sit them upright. If they become unconscious, start CPR. Do not give any other medications at home. Hospitalisation for further care.
precautions: Do not take any more of the suspected medication
Do not delay – severe reactions can progress rapidly
Do not give oral antihistamines as the primary treatment
If the person has a history of drug allergy, inform the team
Prepare for emergency treatment
